demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Physical pain in a part of the body

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something about me that made the event happen
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

vignette: Arthur stood in the dappled shade of the pine stand, chainsaw humming, when the branch above him caught the wind. He had misjudged the tension, and the limb tore free with a sickening crack, careening downward. He remembered the wet thud against the volunteer's thigh, the sudden silence, and the way his own hands had shaken so violently he nearly dropped the equipment. At fifty-four, Arthur had spent decades mastering the timberlands, but in the months that followed, the physical world of the forest had become a minefield. The familiar, dull ache in his right shoulder-a legacy of years hauling logs-suddenly felt like a warning. When colleagues or visitors came too close during site inspections, the victim's pale, stricken face would materialize behind his eyes. These sudden alerts would immediately pull the accident from his mind, replaying the moment the limb had fallen with unrelenting clarity. Each time that familiar ache in his shoulder flared or a crew member invaded his personal space, it instantly triggered a physiological cascade of threat, leaving him unable to relax even in his own cabin. These trigger responses quickly cemented his quiet conviction that there was something intrinsically faulty about him, that he could no longer rely on himself, and that he was no longer capable of the skilled work that had defined him. The unyielding tension cast everyone around him as a potential danger, making him watch other people closely for signs that they might harm him, which amplified his sensitivity to proximity and physical strain. Because he remained so perpetually on guard, scanning for danger whenever strangers approached in the supply depot or down at the local hardware store, he was entirely unable to let the event fade, and the threat monitoring kept the original accident looping vividly in his mind. When the memories finally surfaced, his body would automatically lock into the felling stance, shoulders hunched and breath catching exactly as they had during the fall. As those recollections broke through, an overwhelming grief would wash over him, quickly followed by a hot, paralyzing rage. Those vivid recollections left him so hyper-vigilant that he began fixating on any hint of physical discomfort or crowded spaces, which in turn acted as new triggers. Living in that unrelenting state of dread systematically eroded his belief in his own reliability and competence, leaving him convinced that his past mistake reflected a permanent break in his character. Over the following months, he withdrew from his crew, letting his wife navigate the household finances and social obligations alone, and stopped carrying the chainsaw entirely. He sought help not because he wanted to forget, but because the loop had become too heavy to carry alone, and he desperately hoped to find a way to trust his own judgment again before it cost him his family or his identity.
